final_candidates.decision_summary: K119A has a very strong LOF-proxy score and is rarely tolerated among covered homologs. The WT residue was verified as K119.
N149A combines the strongest pathogenicity prediction in the pool with strong evolutionary intolerance and excellent MSA coverage. The WT residue was verified as N149.
R266A has a strong LOF-proxy prediction and low evolutionary tolerance at a well-covered position. The WT residue was verified as R266.

stop_reason.detail: All four available tool calls have been used, and the accumulated evidence is sufficient to select the final mutations.

history.rationale: K119 is the catalytic PLP-Schiff-base lysine. Removing its reactive side chain should directly abolish catalysis while minimally perturbing the backbone.

K119A has an exceptionally strong pathogenicity prediction and alanine is uncommon at this well-covered position. Its established catalytic-site rationale makes it the leading activity-null candidate.
The annotation fallback supplies no position-specific information, so the strong phenotype and conservation evidence remain decisive.
T257 lies in the highly conserved PLP-active-site region and contributes to cofactor/substrate positioning. Alanine removes its hydroxyl group with limited steric disruption.
T257A has strong predicted pathogenicity, but alanine occurs in nearly one quarter of covered homologs. That evolutionary tolerance substantially weakens the expectation of complete activity loss.
No position-specific annotation was returned, leaving its moderate LOF case unchanged.
R266 is an active-site residue implicated in PLP-dependent catalytic organization. Its substitution by alanine should eliminate key electrostatic interactions while potentially preserving folding.
R266A combines strong predicted damage with low alanine frequency and excellent homolog coverage. Removal of a charged side chain in the catalytic core is a plausible route to abolishing activity.
The contextual fallback neither strengthens nor materially contradicts the existing LOF evidence.
G307S is expected to disrupt a conformationally constrained catalytic-region site. The small substitution is likely compatible with protein production but strongly detrimental to activity.
G307S remains plausible because it is predicted damaging and serine is uncommon among aligned homologs. Its evidence is weaker than that of the leading catalytic-core candidates.
The fallback annotation does not change the balance between evolutionary intolerance and a weaker pathogenicity prediction.
Y223 is positioned in the catalytic domain and its hydroxyl group may support active-site hydrogen bonding. Phenylalanine selectively removes that functionality while retaining aromatic packing.

Although phenylalanine is absent among covered homologs, the conservative substitution has the weakest pathogenicity prediction in the pool. It is less likely than the alternatives to abolish CBS activity.

rejection.reason: Although phenylalanine is absent among covered homologs, the conservative substitution has the weakest pathogenicity prediction in the pool. It is less likely than the alternatives to abolish CBS activity.

history.rationale: N149 is near the PLP-binding catalytic core and may help organize cofactor-associated interactions. Alanine should disrupt those contacts without introducing a bulky or charged residue.

N149A moves to second because it has the strongest pathogenicity score and low alanine frequency under excellent MSA coverage. Confidence remains below K119A because pathogenicity is only a proxy for catalytic loss.
No informative annotation was available to alter its high ranking.
T260 is adjacent to T257 in the glycine-rich active-site segment. Removing its hydroxyl group may impair PLP positioning while maintaining local steric compatibility.
Only moderate predicted pathogenicity and appreciable natural alanine frequency argue against reliable complete loss of activity. It is retained as a lower-priority catalytic-region hypothesis.
The non-specific annotation cannot overcome its comparatively weak pathogenicity signal.
R336 lies within the conserved catalytic domain and likely stabilizes local electrostatic or substrate-binding interactions. Alanine removes these interactions without adding conformational strain.

R336A is predicted to be strongly damaging, but evolutionary evidence is poorly applicable because very few homologs cover this position. It remains a secondary candidate pending functional-site evidence.
The annotation result is uninformative, and low evolutionary coverage prevents promotion despite a strong pathogenicity prediction.
D376 is a conserved acidic residue in the catalytic-domain core. Neutralization may strongly disrupt an essential interaction while avoiding a charge reversal.

The pathogenicity prediction is very strong, but the MSA result has only 10% coverage and therefore provides little dependable positional evidence. Lack of a comparably direct catalytic rationale keeps it outside the Top-3.
Its strong pathogenicity proxy remains promising, but weak MSA coverage continues to limit confidence.
H65 is an axial ligand of the regulatory heme in human CBS. Alanine should disrupt heme coordination and may severely compromise productive enzyme function, though residual activity is possible.

H65A has moderate-to-strong predicted damage and low alanine frequency with complete MSA coverage. It remains below catalytic-domain candidates because disruption at this N-terminal position may not reliably eliminate catalysis.
Its ranking remains unchanged because the new evidence lacks residue-level applicability.
